title: Choosing your five
hook: pick five practices from this camp that actually fit your life

segments.voice: Yesterday, a window, a lamp and a pause. Your line was the day turns. Did you light the lamp by hand? Day one hundred fifty-three.

Picture a toolbox that's been filling up for eight weeks. Breathing: the long exhale, the double sigh, the box. The morning preview and the evening review. Two columns, mine and not mine. Three good things. The view from a mile up, and memento mori. Walking, the body scan, a bedtime. One act of service a week. The phone in a drawer. The sunset. That's a lot of tools. Nobody uses all of them, and trying to would turn peace into a to-do list. The final week of this camp is about making it yours. Today's practice is choosing your five.
screen: `A TOOLBOX, EIGHT WEEKS FULL.` → `NOT ALL OF THEM.` → `CHOOSING YOUR FIVE.`

segments.voice: The Roman philosopher Seneca, in one of his early letters to his friend Lucilius, warns against a certain kind of restless reading: dipping into book after book, never staying with any. A person who is everywhere, he says, is nowhere. Better to spend real time with a few, and let them sink in. Practices work the same way. Five you actually do will change you more than twenty you admire. So how do you choose? Three questions. First, which ones did you actually enjoy? Not the ones you think you should like. The ones where something in you said yes. Second, which ones fit your real life, not your ideal life? If mornings are chaos with small kids, the morning preview may need to wait, and the evening review may fit instead. If you walk the dog anyway, walking meditation is already half done. Third, and this one is powerful, attach each practice to something you already do. Psychologists call this an implementation intention: when this happens, I'll do that. When the kettle boils, three long exhales. When I lie down, the scan. When the sun sets, the lamp. Studies since the late nineteen nineties have found that a plan in this form makes people noticeably more likely to follow through. And here's the heart of today. These five aren't a prescription. Nobody on this path is telling you what to believe or exactly how to live. The practices came from Stoics, Buddhists, Jews, Christians, Sikhs, scientists, a man in the woods in Concord. The five you choose are yours, not mine.
screen: `EVERYWHERE IS NOWHERE.` · `WHICH DID YOU ENJOY?` · `WHICH FIT YOUR REAL LIFE?` · `WHEN THIS, THEN THAT.` · then, large: `YOURS, NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your five. Settle, and breathe. Let the camp's practices drift by, one at a time, and notice which ones make you lean in. Pick five. For each, find an anchor: when, or after what, will it happen? Say each one inside as a sentence: when I, then I. If you get stuck at three, that's fine. Three is a start. The bell holds the time.
Choosing your five. Five practices from this camp that fit your real life, each tied to something you already do. Today's word.
Your line: yours, not mine. Today, write your five down, each with its anchor: when this, then that. Keep the list where you'll see it. Day one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: People building a personal practice usually choose a handful of habits rather than many, and tie each one to an existing moment in the day, like waking, a meal, a walk or bedtime.
